extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism/history; practicing journalists interested in professional and editorial standards
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts standards, virtues, and evaluative criteria for journalism and newspaper editing as articulated in a historical chapter on post‑Civil War American journalism. Emphasizes editorial character, professional skills, ethics, commercial pressures, and the press's civic role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courageous independence and integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: "A courageous independence and integrity of purpose, coupled with a fearless expression of truth as to all public individuals, corporations and parties, are the features in its character to be most encouraged."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a central virtue for the press: journalism should fearlessly expose wrongs and assert the truth about public actors. Anti-patterns include subserviency, indifference, or fear to encounter prosecution and loss of patronage; the press must be willing to risk legal or financial consequences to uphold public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press as instrument to fight corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: "The press really seems to be the best, if not the only instrument, with which honest men can fight these enemies of order and integrity in government and security in property."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The press's role is framed as an active civic instrument for exposing corruption (example: Bowles's attacks on Fisk). Guidance implies investigative zeal and public advocacy against corruption; scoring favors outlets that expose malfeasance even when politically risky.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint and competence in reporting public men and measures
rubrics_metrics.description: "My own observation is that the Press rarely does injustice to a thoroughly honest man... with reference to public men and measures, its knowledge is more intimate and competent than that of any other agency possibly can be; and I know that it withholds unjustly to the public one hundred times, where it speaks wrongly once of the individual."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion balances assertiveness about public affairs with caution about private individuals: be well-informed and competent on public matters, but avoid hasty personal attacks. The text notes libel suits are often brought by exposed fraudsters, suggesting careful documentation of public charges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial transparency and answerability (personal journalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Personal journalism cannot be escaped... whether the one-man power emanates from the counting room or the editorial room... it must be clear and answerable, responsive to the common weal, and, above all, trustworthy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspapers should have a visible, identifiable leadership (editor/owner) who can be held accountable. Anti-patterns: anonymous, opaque control or a paper that pretends to be impersonal while hiding influence. Emphasizes public confidence and legal/ethical accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial competence and managerial versatility
rubrics_metrics.description: "The great editor... ought to be able to write and must be a judge of writing. The newspaper office is a little kingdom. The able editor needs to know and does know every range of it between the editorial room, the composing room and the pressroom... able quickly to sift, detect and discriminate; of varied knowledge, experience and interest."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative standard for editors: broad operational knowledge, literary judgment, newsroom management skills, quick judgment and discernment across all paper functions. Practical expectation: editors should have risen through the ranks and understand technical and editorial workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterestedness and refusal of preferment/bribery
rubrics_metrics.description: "Disinterestedness being the soul of successful journalism, unselfish devotion to the noble purpose in public and private life, he should say to preferment as to bribery, 'Get behind me, Satan.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical standard: editors and papers should avoid personal enrichment, patronage, or political preferment that compromises independence. Measured by willingness to reject bribes/offers that would influence coverage; public trust is paramount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit content to the spirit of the times (commercial responsiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Not so much the views of the editors as the news that the papers contained would sell papers, and all of them made their papers successful by fitting their publications to the spirit of the times."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A pragmatic criterion: successful papers adapt content to what readers want. Guidance emphasizes balancing public service with market realities. Anti-pattern: letting commercial pressures wholly dictate ethics—risk of 'purely commercial morality' unless checked by ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid catering to vanity/snobocracy and disproportionate coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of the younger Bennett: the paper's "fatal defect as a journal was... catering to the vanity of snobocracy... he treated the news from an angle that frequently produced disproportions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid privileging elite social vanity or giving undue prominence/omission based on status. Examples of bad practice include altering content for personal affronts or social snobbery (e.g., omitting a dignitary's name). Evaluate balance and proportionality of coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalism as art and literary sensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: "Art comes into journalism late... Charles Anderson Dana made of journalism an art."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion values literary quality, cultural and intellectual breadth, and stylistic/artistic elements in journalism—not merely factual recording. Encourages cultivated prose, editorial creativity, and high standards of taste, while warning of potential errors of judgment from temperament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspapers' political influence and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: "Newspapers were hereafter to play a direct part in government through their influence on those extra-constitutional forces, the political parties... The paper with the largest circulation was necessarily the most influential... these facts, together with the increased cost of manufacturing a newspaper, would tend toward a purely commercial morality, were it not for the check that lies in the newspaper of small circulation but stiff idealism."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the degree to which a paper exerts political influence responsibly: look for independence from party patronage, character/value of ownership, and presence of small, idealistic outlets that check commercial tendencies. Negative indicators include overt party control and mercenary editorial policies.
